verdict.rationale: Queried against the live corpus the salvation vocabulary is dense and spread across the whole Bible (pan-canonical), with the word for 'save' (sozo) at 436 occurrences in 101 New Testament verses, and 'believe' (pisteuo) at 980 in 217, yet every recorded conversion attaches deliverance to believing, confessing, and crying out, never to a fixed wording. Luke 18:13 has the tax collector say 'God be propitiated toward me the sinner' (Ho theos, hilastheti moi to hamartolo), where 'be propitiated' (hilaskomai) is a near-hapax (a word that occurs only once, or here just 4 times in only 2 verses), a spontaneous penitent cry while beating his breast, and Jesus calls him justified. Romans 10:9-10 conditions 'you will be saved' (sothese) on confessing 'Jesus is Lord' (kyrion Iesoun) and believing that God raised him, content not form. Acts 16:31 answers 'what must I do to be saved' (ti me dei poiein hina sotho) with the bare command 'Believe!' (Pisteuson), supplying no prayer text. The complicating chain Acts 2:21 and Romans 10:13 quotes Joel and uses 'to call upon' (epikaleo), but 'to call upon' (epikaleo) is two-sensed in the canon, a legal appeal as in Acts 25:11 'I appeal to Caesar' (Kaisara epikaloumai) versus calling on the Lord, and Romans 10:14 places calling downstream of believing, so the act is commanded while its words stay free. 1 John 5:13 grounds assurance in the present participle 'those who go on believing' (pisteuousin), ongoing belief, supporting the warning clause. Both halves hold.

scripture.force: The tax collector says 'God be propitiated toward me the sinner' (Ho theos, hilastheti moi to hamartolo). The verb 'be propitiated' (hilaskomai) is verified in the corpus as near unique, only 4 occurrences across just 2 verses, here and Hebrews 2:17, so this is the lone Gospel instance and its sense is fixed by context. He stands afar off, will not lift his eyes, and beats his breast with 'he kept striking' (etupte), an ongoing or repeated past action (imperfect). The cry is spontaneous contrition, not a recited script, and Jesus declares this man went down justified. The force is that a genuine penitent cry, not a set wording, is what is commended.

Verified text reads 'if you confess with your mouth Jesus as Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved' (ean homologeses en to stomati sou kyrion Iesoun kai pisteuses en te kardia sou hoti ho theos auton egeiren ek nekron, sothese). The 'if-then' clause (conditional) 'if' (ean) plus two completed-action subjunctives (aorist subjunctives) makes salvation hinge on the confessed content, 'Jesus is Lord' (kyrion Iesoun), and the believed content, the resurrection, not on the form of any prayer. The instrument is christological belief and confession, which supports the permissibility clause of the proposition.

'with the heart it is believed unto righteousness, and with the mouth it is confessed unto salvation' (Kardia pisteuetai eis dikaiosynen, stomati de homologeitai eis soterian) pairs inner faith with outward confession as two sides of one response. Both verbs are present passive, describing a settled state and its expression rather than a one-time recital. This grounds salvation in believing and confessing rather than in the wording of a formula.

The jailer asks 'what must I do to be saved' (ti me dei poiein hina sotho). The 'it is necessary' (dei) plus infinitive frame openly invites a method answer, which makes the reply that follows a clean test of whether Scripture supplies a fixed procedure.

Verified text gives the bare completed-action command (aorist imperative) 'Believe on the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household' (Pisteuson epi ton kyrion Iesoun, kai sothese su kai ho oikos sou). No prayer wording is supplied, only the command 'Believe!' (pisteuson) on the Lord Jesus with the household result clause. The absence of any prescribed verbal formula at the very point a method was requested is itself the lexical datum against treating a fixed sinner's prayer as the required instrument.

'For everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved' (Pas gar hos an epikalesetai to onoma kyriou sothesetai) quotes Joel, and the parallel Acts 2:21 carries the identical clause. Corpus traversal shows 'to call upon' (epikaleo) is two-sensed across its 93 occurrences, a legal appeal as in Acts 25:11 'I appeal to Caesar' (Kaisara epikaloumai) and the calling on the Lord of 1 Corinthians 1:2 and 2 Timothy 2:22. Here the invocation sense is fixed by 'the name of the Lord' (to onoma kyriou), and Romans 10:14 places calling downstream of believing with 'how shall they call on him in whom they have not believed' (pos epikalesontai eis hon ouk episteusan), so the verb describes the act of calling in faith and leaves its wording open. It commends a real cry without canonizing any set formula.

Verified text reads 'These things I have written to you so that you may know that you have eternal life, to you who go on believing in the name of the Son of God' (Tauta egrapsa hymin hina eidete hoti zoen echete aionion, tois pisteuousin eis to onoma tou huiou tou theou). The present participle 'those who go on believing' (pisteuousin) and present indicative (ongoing, simple statement of fact) 'you have' (echete) locate assurance in ongoing believing, not in a single past act of saying a prayer. This is the lexical anchor for the warning clause, that assurance resting on a one-time formula apart from continued faith and fruit is misplaced.

'Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved' (Pas hos ean epikalesetai to onoma kyriou sothesetai) repeats the Joel citation at Pentecost. The same future passive 'will be saved' (sothesetai) and the same invocation idiom appear, confirming that the saving act is calling on the Lord, an act recorded with varied words across the canon rather than one prescribed sentence.

The Hebrew at Joel 3:5 in the Masoretic numbering reads 'everyone who calls on the name of YHWH will be delivered' (kol asher yiqra beshem YHWH yimmalet), using 'to call' (qara), which the corpus shows occurs 735 times. Acts 2:21 and Romans 10:13 quote this verse, so the New Testament invocation is rooted in an Old Testament pattern, 'to call on the name of YHWH' (liqro beshem YHWH) at Genesis 4:26, Psalm 116:4 and 13, and Zephaniah 3:9, none of which fixes a wording. The act of calling is spread across the whole Bible (pan-canonical), the formula is not.

complicating_texts.resolution: 'For everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved' (Pas gar hos an epikalesetai to onoma kyriou sothesetai) could be read as endorsing a verbal invocation that a fixed sinner's prayer formalizes. Corpus traversal of 'to call upon' (epikaleo) across its 93 occurrences shows two attested senses, a legal appeal as in Acts 25:11 'I appeal to Caesar' (Kaisara epikaloumai) and the invocation of the Lord in 1 Corinthians 1:2 and 2 Timothy 2:22. Context here fixes the invocation sense by 'the name of the Lord' (to onoma kyriou), and Romans 10:14 makes calling depend on prior believing, so 'to call upon' (epikaleo) names the act of calling in faith and leaves the words free. It supports a genuine cry while not requiring or canonizing any set formula.

Because 'with the mouth it is confessed' (stomati homologeitai) is joined to 'unto salvation' (soterian), the verse can be pressed to make a spoken confession the saving instrument, edging toward a formula. The present passive verbs and the parallel 'with the heart it is believed' (kardia pisteuetai) show confession as the outward expression of inward faith, one response viewed from two sides, which preserves the permissibility clause without supporting a saving recital.

'Rise, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on his name' (Anastas baptisai kai apolousai tas hamartias sou epikalesamenos to onoma autou) pairs the completed-action middle participle (aorist middle participle) of 'to call upon' (epikaleo) with baptism, and could be read as making the spoken invocation a cleansing act. The participle is contemporaneous calling on the Lord that accompanies the response of faith, and like the other 'to call upon' (epikaleo) texts it specifies no fixed wording, so it commends a real invocation without prescribing a formula.

variants.note: Direct query confirms the 116 ingested ECM apparatus (critical edition of New Testament textual variants) units are all in 3 John chapter 1, and none of the anchor verses Luke 18:13, Romans 10:9, Romans 10:10, Acts 16:30, Acts 16:31, 1 John 5:13 lie in that window, so 'not in ECM scope' (not_in_ecm_scope) is honest. The editorial sigla marked in the SBLGNT text of these verses touch word order, a pronoun, and completed-action (aorist) or future spelling, none of which alters 'save' (sozo), 'believe' (pisteuo), 'confess' (homologeo), 'be propitiated' (hilaskomai), or 'call upon' (epikaleo), so the verdict holds across plausible readings.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: The verb forms tie salvation to believing, confessing, and calling out, and tie assurance to present continuous believing in 1 John 5:13. No recorded conversion supplies a fixed prayer wording, and the bare command 'Believe!' (Pisteuson) at Acts 16:31 withholds any script at the exact point a method was sought, so the words support the proposition's two halves.

A reading that isolates 'with the mouth it is confessed unto salvation' (stomati homologeitai eis soterian) in Romans 10:10 and 'calls on the name of the Lord' (epikalesetai to onoma kyriou) in Romans 10:13 and Acts 2:21, with the baptismal 'calling on' (epikalesamenos) of Acts 22:16, can make a spoken invocation the saving instrument and so treat a set prayer as the prescribed means. In its strongest form this lens reads the mouth confession and the calling as the very point at which salvation is enacted, which is the most that the formula position can claim from the vocabulary.

Read by progressive revelation (the unfolding of truth across the canon over time), Acts 2:21 and Romans 10:13 quote Joel, whose Hebrew 'call on the name of YHWH' (qara beshem YHWH) runs back through Genesis 4:26, Psalm 116, and Zephaniah 3:9. The Old to New Testament arc shows a single act, calling on the name of the Lord in faith, with consistently varied wording, which strongly supports the act while denying any canonized formula.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict rests on the grammatical force of the verbs across the anchor pericopes (units of text) read together by 'the analogy of Scripture' (analogia scripturae), the principle that Scripture interprets Scripture, the near-unique 'be propitiated' (hilaskomai) cry in Luke 18:13, the bare command 'Believe!' (Pisteuson) in Acts 16:31, the present participle 'those who go on believing' (pisteuousin) in 1 John 5:13, and the two-sensed 'to call upon' (epikaleo) whose invocation sense is fixed by 'the name of the Lord' (to onoma kyriou) and made dependent on prior belief by Romans 10:14. Progressive revelation (the unfolding of truth across the canon over time) is marked because the New Testament invocation quotes and extends the Old Testament Joel pattern.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: What does Scripture identify as the means by which a person is saved and gains assurance, and does any cited text prescribe a fixed verbal prayer as that means or as the ground of assurance?
stem_audit.notes: The stem uses the extra-biblical methodological label 'sinner's prayer' and frames a normative pastoral judgment with the evaluative terms permissible and dangerous, which preloads a verdict. The lexical engine cannot rule on pastoral permissibility, only on whether the cited texts make a fixed prayer formula the saving or assuring instrument. The verdict is derived on the original stem by testing that lexical sub-question, which the words answer cleanly. The label 'sinner's prayer' itself does not occur in the lexical store. VERDICT-CHANGED: no, verdict unchanged from the prior file, affirms remains true, and the deeper queries strengthen rather than alter it.

lay_summary: The texts behind this question describe how a person is saved and how a believer comes to assurance, and the original word forms point away from any fixed prayer script. In Luke 18:13 the tax collector cries 'be merciful to me, the sinner' while beating his breast and refusing to lift his eyes. That word for 'be merciful' or 'be propitiated' (hilaskomai in Greek) is almost unique in the whole New Testament, appearing only here and one other place, and the cry is a spontaneous plea of sorrow, not a recited form, yet Jesus calls that man justified. In Romans 10:9-10 salvation is joined to believing in the heart and confessing with the mouth (the words used are 'believe' or pisteuo and 'confess' or homologeo) that Jesus is Lord and that God raised him from the dead. The focus is the content believed and the person confessed, not the wording of a prayer. In Acts 16:31, when the jailer asks what he must do to be saved, the answer is simply the command 'Believe!' (Pisteuson) on the Lord Jesus, and no prayer text is given for him to repeat. So the part of the statement that allows a prayer when it carries real repentance and faith matches the pattern, because what counts is genuine belief and confession rather than a memorized sentence. The one place a reader might press for a set formula is the line 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved', quoted from Joel in Acts 2:21 and Romans 10:13. But the verb for calling (epikaleo) carries two senses across the canon, a legal appeal, as when Paul appeals to Caesar, and a trusting cry to the Lord, and Romans 10:14 says people cannot call on one they have not first believed. So calling is the overflow of faith, and its words stay open. The warning side also matches. First John 5:13 says these things were written so that those who go on believing (the present participle pisteuousin) may know they have eternal life, and the verbs for believing and having life are ongoing present forms, which places assurance in a faith that continues rather than in a single past moment of saying a prayer.
